content.title: How to Watch the Artemis II Mission Land Back on Earth
content.text: The historic Artemis II mission is about to come to an end. The 10-day mission by a crew of four astronauts took them around the moon and deeper into space than any humans in history. It's set to wrap up on April 10 with the crew's return to Earth by splashing down in the Pacific Ocean. Here's what to know and how to watch their return. When Will the Artemis Crew Return to Earth? The crew of NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen began preparing on April 9 for their return by reviewing re-entry and splashdown procedures, according to NASA. They were about 147,337 miles from Earth on Thursday morning, per NASA. The Orion capsule containing the astronauts is scheduled to splash down in the Pacific Ocean about 50 miles off the coast of San Diego at 8:07 p.m. ET on April 10. How Can You Watch the Orion Capsule Splashdown in the Ocean? NASA will livestream the spacecraft's return on its YouTube channel. How Are the Artemis II Crew and NASA Preparing for Their Return to Earth?In addition to reviewing procedures, they also reinstalled the seats in the Orion capsule to make sure all the items are secure upon their reentry into the Earth's atmosphere, according to NASA. A joint NASA and Department of Defense team in California has been rehearsing to quickly retrieve the crew from the ocean upon splashdown. The U.S.S. John P. Murtha has been approaching the splashdown zone in the Pacific Ocean in preparation. Dr. Jesse Wang is the lead of the medical team that will examine the crew upon their return. "We will enter the capsule, make sure the astronauts are OK," Wang said on TODAY April 9. "Render any medical aid as necessary and extract them from the capsule." Helicopters and a team of U.S. Navy divers in small boats will make their way to the Orion capsule and then install an inflatable collar around it to stabilize the spacecraft in the ocean waves, per NASA. The divers will install an inflatable raft under the capsule's side hatch to help in retrieving the astronauts. The crew will then be individually lifted on to a helicoper and returned to the main ship. Two helicopters will retrieve two crew members apiece. It's expected to take about two hours before the crew is secured and returned to the medical bay for inspection by Wang's team. The Orion capsule will be towed and stored in the well deck of the ship. NASA will also have multiple aircraft that will be tracking the Orion capsule's 13-minute journey that begins about 75 miles above the Earth's surface. What Is the Artemis II's Reentry Speed?The Orion capsule will exceed speeds of 20,000 miles per hour upon reeentry and will temporarily lose communication with NASA for about six minutes as plasma intensifies around the capsule. The spacecraft will slow from speeds of nearly 25,000 miles per hour to 300 miles per hour during reentry before a system of parachutes deploys for a 20-mile-per-hour splashdown, according to NASA. This is one of the most dangerous parts of the entire mission due to the speeds and temperatures experienced by the crew. The Orion spacecraft's heat shield, which protects the astronauts from temperatures of more than 5,000 degrees in the 16.5-foot-wide capsule, has had past issues. Part of the heat shield's material cracked during a test flight as part of the unmanned Artemis I mission in 2022, which a NASA investigation found caused "some charred material to break off in several locations.” The heat shield remains the same on the Artemis II mission because it had already been built by the time NASA discovered the flaw in the heat shield. In order to mitigate risk, NASA has altered the Orion's reentry path to Earth to lessen the time it is exposed to extreme temperatures. Amit Kshatriya, NASA’s associate administrator, said at a news briefing on April 9 that he has "high confidence" the heat shield will hold up upon reentry thanks to the altered flight path. How Will the Artemis II Astronauts Get Back to Earth?The service module will separate about 20 minutes before Orion reaches the upper atmosphere southeast of Hawaii. The Orion spacecraft with then perform a series of roll maneuvers for safety reasons, according to NASA. Orion will deploy its drogue parachutes near 22,000 feet and then three more parachutes at 6,000 feet for the capsule to softly land in the Pacific Ocean. During reentry, the astronauts will be seated and wearing their pressurized spacesuits, which will regulate their temperature. The capsule will face reentry temperatures nearly 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is about half as hot as the surface of the sun.
